watch/walk: Training walks the weights downhill on the loss, L, one step at a time, like the ball walking down the bowl.
watch/blind: A real model has millions of weights, so there is no bowl to see. What you can see is how high the ball is: every hundred steps, training prints the loss.
watch/log: That printout is the training log: log as in a ship's log, a record kept along the way, not a logarithm.
watch/curve: Plot each reading against its step, and you have a loss curve. Its shape tells you what is wrong, and what to change.
rates/two: Why do the shapes differ? Take a loss with just two weights, rising gently with one and steeply with the other: two bowls, each with its own ball.
rates/sum: The loss is their two heights added up, so one curve tracks both balls at once.
rates/low: With a rate too low, both balls creep. The loss falls slowly, by about the same small amount each step: almost a straight line.
rates/good: A good rate: the steep ball slides straight in, and the gentle one follows. The loss drops fast, then keeps creeping lower.
rates/high: Too high is subtler. The gentle ball still slides in, but for the steep bowl this rate is right at the edge: each step flips its ball to the other wall, at the same height.
rates/plateau: So the loss drops fast, then stalls high: a plateau, flat high ground. The steps are too big to settle into the bottom.
rates/huge: Far too high, and the steep ball lands farther out every step: the walk diverges. The loss shoots up, until the arithmetic breaks down and prints nan: not a number.
rates/order: So from the lowest rate to the highest: a slow straight line, a fast drop that keeps going, a fast drop that stalls, and a blow-up.
rates/cure: The shape names the cure. A slow line wants a bigger rate; a plateau or a blow-up wants a smaller one.
rates/bengio: Yoshua Bengio, in 2012, called the learning rate often the single most important setting to tune. His advice when training diverges: try again with a rate three times smaller.
more/noisy: Another shape comes from the batch. In a small batch, each gradient comes from a few examples and scatters, so the loss jitters up and down while its trend still falls.
more/big: A bigger batch scatters less, and the curve smooths out.
more/val: Now add the validation loss, measured on held-back examples. If training keeps falling while validation turns and climbs, the model is overfitting.
read/list: Often the log is only numbers. Read them as a curve, one point per reading: here, every hundred steps.
read/slow: Each reading is about two hundredths below the last: the same small drop every time, a straight line. The rate is too low.
read/plateau: This one falls fast, from two point three oh to one point three eight, then hovers near one point two: a plateau. The rate is too high.
read/explode: This one more than doubles every reading, until it prints nan. The rate is far too high.
read/noisy: This one goes up, down, up, down, but each low is lower than the last: noisy, and still trending down. The batch is too small.
read/val: To find where to stop, read the validation losses. Logged every two epochs, they bottom out at one point one nine, the fourth reading.
read/epoch: With two epochs between readings, the fourth one is epoch eight, not epoch four. Those are the weights to keep.
